# 65B That Outperformed 501B: Inside Ripple-65B's $32 Million Bet Against Scale

The large language model industry has spent the last two years moving in one direction: more parameters, more experts, more money. Ricursive Intelligence went the other way. Their Ripple-65B Preview—a dense transformer with 65 billion parameters—scored 80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 on November 4, 2026, beating open American models 8, 12, and even 15 times its size. On a $32 million budget. This is not just another release. It is a bet that architectural efficiency matters more than brute force.

## From Chips to Language

Ricursive Intelligence is not a startup out of nowhere. The company was founded by Anna Goldie (CEO) and Azalia Mirhoseini (CTO)—researchers who, at Google, were instrumental in creating AlphaChip, a reinforcement learning system for chip floorplanning. The logic of moving from silicon to language models is direct: if you know how to optimize the placement of billions of transistors, you understand how to optimize computation. In January 2026, Ricursive raised a $300 million Series A at a $4 billion valuation—with Nvidia, Lightspeed, and Sequoia among the investors. Ripple-65B Preview is not a standalone product but a public "general-purpose" version of the internal model already used in their chip design platform.

## Density as a Deliberate Choice

While competitors build sparse Mixture-of-Experts architectures, where only a fraction of parameters activates per token, Ricursive chose the opposite. In Ripple-65B, all 65 billion parameters fire on every token. This is more expensive computationally but cheaper in infrastructure: no need to balance experts, no need to manage complex routing. The model uses a "thin-and-deep" architecture: a narrow residual stream of width 5120 and 80 layers—proportions that typically yield better reasoning performance at a fixed parameter budget. The shift from a Llama-like architecture (Olmo 3) to a Gemma 3N-like one was made for training stability at scale. The result is a dense model that fits all 65 billion parameters on consumer-grade hardware like NVIDIA DGX Spark.

## The Tech Stack: Five Decisions That Delivered 16x

The architectural changes in Ripple-65B are not cosmetic. Each targets a specific weakness of standard transformers. First, **overprovisioned attention heads**: more heads than typical models of this size, directly strengthening reasoning ability. Second, **an increased ratio of sliding-window to global attention** while simultaneously reducing the SWA window—the model looks at the entire sequence more often, not just local context. Third, **FFN activation clipping**—limiting activations in feed-forward layers for training stability and efficiency. Fourth, **gated attention**—a gating mechanism to control information flow between layers. And fifth, **global NoPE** (No Positional Embeddings at the global level) combined with local RoPE—a hybrid positional encoding scheme that works better on long contexts.

The combined effect of these decisions is measured not in percentages but in multiples. Relative to the Olmo 3 baseline, the model improved compute efficiency on code by **16x**, and on the final "hero run" by **55x**. In other words, the same result is achieved with far fewer FLOPs. That is exactly what allowed them to stay within budget.

## $32 Million and 1.4 Million Rollouts

The $32 million figure is central to the Ripple-65B story. Ricursive claims this sum covers **all** R&D costs: from building the pretraining ladder and data mixing to synthetic generation, debugging, post-training recipes, and final runs. For comparison: the previous open leader in agentic coding cost roughly ten times more, according to the company's estimate. Sam Altman said in 2023 that training GPT-4 cost more than $100 million, and Dario Amodei predicted frontier model costs of $10–100 billion by 2026–2027. Ripple-65B is a counterargument to that trajectory.

The savings do not come from training less. The model went through **12 trillion tokens** of pretraining on 8K sequences, then 200 billion tokens of midtraining on 64K, 6.5 billion tokens of long-context on 2M, 183 billion tokens of SFT, and a final stage of mixed RL. The savings come from efficiency at each stage. For post-training, Ricursive needed only **1.4 million RL rollouts** to reach 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1—roughly 70 times fewer than Reflection Beam required. Instead of buying post-training data, the team built its own synthetic pipelines with quality and coverage filtering.

## The Result: More Than Terminal-Bench

80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 is the headline, but not the only metric. On SWE-Bench Pro v2.0 Hard, the model scored **79.1%**, beating Reflection Beam 501B (72.4%) and Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (39.6%). On DeepSWE 1.1—**44.3%** versus Beam's 43.3%. At the same time, on some other benchmarks Ripple trails larger competitors: on MCP Atlas—71.67% versus 85.4% for Inkling 2 Small; on DeepSWE—44.3% versus 72.1%. Ricursive does not hide these numbers, and that adds credibility: the model is strong precisely in the tasks it was trained for—agentic coding and terminal work.

What matters more than absolute numbers is the comparison with size. Ripple-65B beats **Reflection Beam 501B** (80.1), **Meta Muse Spark Open 816B** (76.4), **Thinking Machines Inkling 975B** (63.8), and **NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B** (56.4) on Terminal-Bench 2.1. A model 15 times smaller than some of them delivers the best result on a specific type of task. This does not mean 65B is always better than 500B. It means that for a narrow class of tasks—agentic coding with strict requirements for local deployment—a dense, optimized architecture can compete with sparse giants.

## What This Changes

The release of Ripple-65B Preview is not about "small models winning." It is about **architecture and training recipe choices ceasing to be secondary to scale**. If $32 million and a team of five can produce a model that beats a 501-billion-parameter competitor on a key benchmark, then the barrier to entry for "open SOTA" drops dramatically. Ricursive's bet is that the next wave of efficiency will come not from even more parameters but from even more precise tuning of how those parameters are used. And if that is true, the question "how many parameters do you have?" will soon give way to "how efficiently do you spend them?" Ripple-65B has already answered that question—and the answer turned out to be unexpectedly modest in number and unexpectedly loud in consequences.

🎬 Someone built an open-source bridge that lets Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other AI agents generate and edit images and videos using your existing Meta Muse account.

It's called Muse4AI, an unofficial Windows application that exposes Muse's creative features through REST, MCP, and OAuth.

The idea is simple: instead of manually switching between your AI coding agent and a video-generation website, let the agent use the service directly.

🤖 What can your agent do?

▪️ Generate images from text prompts and reference photos.

▪️ Create AI videos and monitor generation progress.

▪️ Edit an existing MP4 using natural-language instructions.

▪️ Extend generated clips while maintaining the same conversation.

▪️ Continue previous chats without losing context.

▪️ Search and organize generated assets in a local library.

▪️ Cancel jobs and inspect their status.

The developer reports support for video extensions across six consecutive steps, potentially reaching around 60 seconds, depending on the original generation.

🔌 Multiple ways to connect

Muse4AI offers three integration methods:

▪️ MCP: For compatible coding agents.

▪️ REST API: For custom scripts, automation, and applications.

▪️ OAuth: For connecting clients with an explicit authorization flow.

That means tools such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and n8n can interact with the same local bridge.

🔐 How does authentication work?

Muse4AI runs on your Windows computer and uses your existing signed-in Muse session.

The application provides a local endpoint:

http://127.0.0.1:47821/mcp

Agents can connect using scoped API keys or OAuth.

In the OAuth flow, the user approves a six-digit code displayed by the application.

Keys can be rate-limited and revoked individually.

The developer says local results, credentials, and job history remain on the user's computer rather than passing through a separate Muse4AI cloud service.

🛠️ Technical details

▪️ Node.js 22+ for building from source.

▪️ Windows installer and desktop application.

▪️ Local asset library, generation queue, and API dashboard.

▪️ MIT-licensed source code.

▪️ Automated test suite containing 775 tests.

⚠️ Important limitations

Muse4AI is not an official Meta product.

The integration automates an existing Muse account, so changes to the website may break functionality.

Automation may also be subject to Meta's terms of service.

And although the bridge runs locally, image and video generation still happens through Meta's hosted service, not on your own GPU.

There is no Muse4AI subscription, but your existing account limits still apply.

macOS and Linux builds haven't been officially tested.

Why is this interesting?

Creative AI tools are becoming components that agents can orchestrate.

A coding agent could generate promotional visuals, inspect them, request revisions, and organize the finished assets without requiring you to manually repeat every step in another application.

 * Overview: Edge-AI startup Underdog officially launched Woof, an ultra-compact 31.7MB text-to-speech foundation model with 31M parameters engineered to execute entirely inside web browsers without cloud servers.

   * Runs client-side in standard browser runtimes with zero internet connectivity or backend server dependency.
   * Instant local voice generation: delivers immediate speech synthesis without cloud roundtrips or recurring token API fees.

 * Key Capabilities:

   * Cross-model memory portability: allows persistent user and project context to travel seamlessly across different coding agents and frontier models without re-prompting.
   * Automatically isolates core project constraints and architectural decisions from noisy, ephemeral reasoning tokens.

Three things I learned building an AI agent for creators during a 10-day hackathon, including what broke.

Billing can stop everything. For days, every Meta Muse call returned “402 Payment Required.” The app fell back to Claude, so it still worked. Now I treat “payment required” as an outage.

Fallbacks are part of the product. When a model goes down, does the user get a blank screen or a clear message? I now design for the message.

Honest labels build trust. The comment-reply loop predates the hackathon, and the demo says so. Viewers notice when claims are precise.

The app drops in a raw video, and Muse Voice transcribes it. Muse Spark writes titles and captions, and Muse Wonder picks the hook. Nico replies to comments in your voice, and Muse Spark checks each reply first.

note_tweet.text:
Meta Muse is launching voice AI features, but nobody asked for them

That’s the exact mood I caught from comments on socials. Meta just rolled out real-time voice calls with AI avatars in Meta Muse. Hundreds of voices, live lip-syncing, interruption support... the tech is technically impressive.
But what I see is a collective “Why?”

Here’s my honest take on it, both as a person who consumes content and as a marketer building in the AI space

1. Wrong thing at wrong time
We’re already living through a wave where AI is replacing jobs and workflows. Pushing AI to now substitute basic human conversation feels tone-deaf to a lot of people

When tech tries to simulate emotional warmth instead of solving actual operational friction, it creates immediate friction with the audience

2. Read the room 
As creators and brand managers, we get excited by what AI can do, but we forget to ask if it should. 

If your core audience is burnt out on ai, forcing more “synthetic intimacy” will backfire

3. If you risk it, fix the positioning 
If Meta framed this purely as a tool for automated customer support training, script testing, or accessibility, the backlash would be half of what it is. Positioning is everything. When you launch a feature with a questionable use, your narrative must be rock-solid: what’s actually use for customer?

At the end of the day, AI shines when it handles the heavy, invisible lifting like data, reporting, so humans can actually spend more time being human

The second AI tries to replace the conversation itself, people pull away.
Curious to hear your thoughts on this💭
